# Introduction

The goal for this guide is to introduce version controlling with Git in the
context of collaborative data analysis projects.

The guide was initially a quick start guide for my Causal Inference group 
project. Since I was the one who proposed we use Git for collaboration, I wanted
to write a step-by-step guide to make the adoption easy. Turns out I grossly
underestimated the difficulty of writing the guide, and couldn't complete it 
before the project deadline. It has now evolved into a more comprehensive 
introduction of Git.

Why yet another Git tutorial, while the internet has no shortage of posts on
the same topic? What makes this guide different?

1. This guide contains crash courses on some fundamental programming/computer
   concepts. Many Git tutorials assume a significant amount of knowledge on 
   programming, and is not approachable for those early in their coding journey. 
   A common approach is to simply instruct readers to copy the commands, paste 
   them to the terminal, press `<Enter>`, and voilà, you get the desired result. 
   But (1) you should *never* run random commands from the internet without 
   understanding what exactly they do, and (2) you have to known them sooner or
   later, so why not now?

   Throughout the guide, you will see block in the following form:

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse=true}
   # Crash Course Example

   Hello there.
   :::
   in which  I provide gentle introductions of new concepts that are relevant 
   to the topic. Click on the green tile bar to see the content.

2. This guide visualizes Git's inner working. In addition to visualizing the
   topology of Git branches (which many tutorials also do), this guide 
   visualize the relation between different Git objects (mostly commits and 
   blobs) to illustrate how Git works in a low level. While not strictly 
   necessary to start using Git, I find having a mental model of how Git work 
   helps distinguish similar Git operations.

   This approach is inspired by 
   [MIT's "The Missing Semester of Your CS Education"](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/version-control/).
   To find the best way to introduce Git, I have read numerous tutorials and 
   blog posts to see how people approach the topic. Most of them jump right into
   the terminal and start executing Git commands. MIT's lecture on Git took
   a bottom-up approach, and started by explaining Git's *data model* on 
   *blackboards* (\*chef's kiss\*). When Git commands were introduced in the
   second half of the lecture, they were merely implementations of the 
   operations to alter the data model introduced earlier. I'm convinced this is
   the superior way to learn Git.

3. This guide helps *me* understand Git better. I've used Git for years. I know
   how to use simple Git commands. I memorize common Git commands. But it wasn't
   until writing this guide that I realize how little I actually know about Git. 
   This also serve as a learning opportunity.

Similar to "The Missing Semester," the guide is split into two sections: in 
Section 2 I provide a high level introduction of Git's data model. I identify
several common problems programmers have while coding, and how Git solve them
by visualizing a simplified Git's data model.[^note-graphs]. In Section 3 I
introduce the actual Git command to make operations introduced in the previous
section possible.

[^note-graphs]: I spent *way* more time making the graphs than writing the text. 
It's the main reason why I couldn't finish it on time. I hope it's freaking 
worth it.

# Why Git

Git is a **version control system (VCS)** that help tracks changes made in text
files. It is commonly used in programming to manage changes made in source code,
but can also be applied to other file formats[^note-vim-application], such as 
Markdown, CSV, etc. 

[^note-vim-application]: In theory Git can also track changes made in non-text 
files, such as compressed files (e.g. Microsoft Word documents) and binary 
files (e.g. SQLite file), but dedicated VCS for these specialized file format is
usually preferred over Git. The reason would be apparent later.

## Version Control

If you have worked on a non-trivial project involving multiple files that went 
through several iterations, the following directory structure should look 
familiar:

```
my-project/
├── data/
│   └── data.csv
├── report.Rmd
├── report-20250101.Rmd
├── report-20250201.Rmd
├── report-20250301.Rmd
├── report-final.Rmd
├── report-final-update-intro.Rmd
├── report-final-version-2.Rmd
├── report-final-version-3.Rmd
└── report-final-version-4-final-final.Rmd
```
 

::: {#cc-directory .callout-tip collapse="true"}
### Crash Course on Directory

Another name for **directory** that people may be more familiar with is 
"folder". While there *may be* some minor differences between the two[^note-folder]
, the distinction is not important for the purpose for this tutorial. Most 
technical documents use "directory," so that's the term I would stick to.

[^note-folder]: Upon research some people have *strong* opinions on directory vs
folder.

Directories are usually represented in tree structures. The above example reads:

- Directory `my-project/` has 10 children: 1 sub-directory `data/` and 9 files in 
the form of `report.Rmd` and `report-xxx.Rmd`
- Directory `data/` has exactly one child -- file `data.csv`.

We say `my-project/` is the **working root directory** of this project. 
Everything concering the project is inside this directory.

Slashes (`/`) are added at the end of directories' names (`my-project/`, 
`data/`) in the text representation above. This is done to distinguish between 
a directory and a file. 

We can also use `/` to specify the **path** of a file or a directory. The path
for `report.Rmd` is `my-project/report.Rmd`, and the path for `data.csv` is 
`my-project/data/data.csv`. 

Note that in practice Windows use back-slashes (`\`) instead of `/`, so the 
examples should be rewritten as `my-project\report.Rmd` and 
`my-project\data\data.csv` if you are using Windows. In most cases Windows 
should be able to understand both notations. MacOS and Linux use `/` natively, 
and this is also what this tutorial use.

There are three special paths:

| notation | meaning               |
| -        | ---                   |
| `./`     | current directory     |
| `../`    | parent directory      |
| `/`      | system root directory |

(On Windows they are `.\`, `..\` and `\` respectively, but as mentioned you can
substitute `\` with `/` in most cases.)

If you are located in `my-project/`, the **relative path** for 
`report.Rmd` would be `./report.Rmd` -- starting from my current directory 
`my-project/`, look for `report.Rmd`. Similarly, the relative path for `data.csv`
would then be `./data/data.csv` -- starting from my current directory 
`my-project/`, look into directory `data/`, then locate file `data.csv`.

If you are located in `data/`, the relative path for `report.Rmd` would
be `./../report.Rmd` -- starting from my current directory `data/`, go to its 
parent directory `my-project/`, then locate file `report.Rmd`. `data.csv`, on
the other hand, is much simpler -- `./data.csv`.

You do not need to explicitly specify `./`. So `./report.Rmd` can be written
simply as `report.Rmd`, and `./../report.Rmd` is equivalent to `../report.Rmd`.

System root directory `/`, sometimes simplified as **root directory**, is the
root directory of your system (duh!). Every file and directory on your system
is a child or descendant of `/`. Paths starting from `/` are **absolute paths**. 
Say `my-project/` is located at `/home/louis/Document/class/causal_inference`,
the absolute path for `data.csv` would then be 
`/home/louis/Document/class/causal_inference/my-project/data/data.csv`.

Relative paths or absolute paths may be preferred depending on your use case.
The rule of thumb is use relative path if it is project specific ("this file 
reads data from a sibling directory"), and absolute path if it is system-wide 
("use R version 4.5.1 on the system to run this script").

---

People used to graphical user interfaces (GUI) may find this unnecessarily 
abstract. Why not just open File Explorer then point and click? 

Firstly, it's easier for technical document writers to include a text 
representation of the directory structure than taking screenshots of File 
Explorer. Secondly, many tools only provide command line interfaces (CLI) -- you 
type commands in a terminal -- and the arguments are expected to be text. While
Git does provided basic graphical user interfaces, and there exist third-party 
tools that provide more advances interfaces, we will start with CLI. 

Understanding path and directory is crucial to programming and development, and
messing up basic concepts can lead to irreversible consequences. My favorite
example is `rm -rf /my-project` vs `rm -rf / my-project`. `rm -rf` deletes 
*everything* is the path provided by the next argument. So the first command
deletes everything in `/my-project`, while the second one delete everything in
`/` (note the space between `/` and `my-project`!) which is... everything in
*your system*!

This exact mistake happen surprisingly often.

It is also a reminder you should *never* blindly run commands found on the 
internet or produced by AI.
:::


You are working on your report, and are instructed to submit your draft to your
supervisor on the first day of each month. For each submission you append your 
report name `report.Rmd` with dates (e.g. `report-20250101.Rmd`)

In April you are ready to submit your report and name your latest iteration 
`report-final.Rmd`. But your supervisor is not satisfied with your intro and
asked you to make some major changes. You update your report, name this new 
report `report-final-update-intro.Rmd` to indicate what you've change. But of
course this is not the only changes you are asked to make. You ditched your
previous naming scheme and give each iteration a version number, e.g. 
`report-final-version-2.Rmd`, until you reach version 4 and
name it `report-final-verions-4-final-final.Rmd`.

This work flow is not optimal. First and foremost, you store multiple copies of
the same file which is not only confusing but also taking many disk space.
For each iteration you create a new copy of the report regardless of the amount
of the changes. You may have only changed a few characters, still a 
near-identical duplicate of the file needs to be created. It is also not obvious
what the differences between each versions are. You *can* be disciplined and 
enforce consistent naming schemes (`report-final-update-intro.Rmd`), or 
maintain a changelog recording what has been changed between iterations 
(`version 3: fixed x-axis in graph 4.1 and 4.2`) , but they add more overheads 
and complexity to your workflow.

Introducing **Git**, a piece of software to make versioning simple
[^note-simple]. Instead of saving multiple versions of the same file, we save 
*snapshots* of each iterations, also known as **commits**.

[^note-simple]: Simple, not easy. While the underlying architecture may be simple, 
(every git operation is either creating some objects or moving `HEAD`!) it has
quite a learning curve and not an easy tool to master.

Consider a todo list `todo.txt` that went through two iterations of changes

:::: {.columns layout-ncol=3}
::: {}
Version 1:

```txt
grocery:
  apple
  banana
```
:::
::: {}
Version 2: 

```txt
grocery:
   apple
   banana
   orange
```

add `orange` to list `grocery`
:::
::: {}
Version 3: 

```txt
grocery:
  banana
  orange
clean:
  dishes
  laundry
```

remove `apple` from `grocery`, and add a new list `clean`
:::
::::

With our primitive manual version control system, we would store three versions
of the todo list:

```txt
todo/
├── todo-version-1.txt 
├── todo-version-2.txt 
└── todo-version-3.txt 
```

With Git, only one todo list is visible to user at a time, Every time we make 
changes to `todo.txt` and commit the changes, Git takes a snapshot of the file 
content and save it in a special storage[^note-storage]. 

[^note-storage]: We'll explain what exactly this "storage" is. For now, just
think of it as a special place where Git stores everything.

```txt
todo/
└── todo.txt 
```

Let's go through a very simple Git workflow.


First, we create `todo.txt`, then add `apple` and `banana` to `grocery` list.
Then we commit the changes with Git, and get commit C1. The commit points to 
version 1 of the file in storage.


```{dot}
{{< include graphs/simple_1.dot >}}
```

Next we add `orange` to list `grocery`. We iterate over commit C1 and
get commit C2, which points to verions 2 of the todo list in the
storage.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/simple_2.dot >}}
```

Finally, we remove `apple` from `grocery`, and add a new list `clean`. Again,
we iterate over commit C2 and get commit C3, which it points to version 3 of 
the todo list.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/simple_3.dot >}}
```


Think of Git as a time machine. We can freely travel between commits, and 
depending on what commit we travel to, Git points to the corresponding version 
of `todo.txt`.

If you travel to C1 and open `todo.txt`, it shows: 

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/travel_1.dot >}}
```

If you travel to C2 and open `todo.txt`, it shows:

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/travel_2.dot >}}
```

If you travel to C3 and open `todo.txt`, it shows

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/travel_3.dot >}}
```

At any given commit, you see exactly one `todo.txt`, but the content changes
accordingly.

While Git *does* create new copies of `todo.txt` for each snapshot, it also
compress them so that it take up less disk space. 

Furthermore, Git doesn't always create new copies for each snapshot. To 
illustrate this, let's revisit our `my-project` example. A naive version control 
system would create new `report.Rmd` and `data.csv` for each commit:

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/naive_0.dot >}}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

1. First we commit `report.Rmd` (version 1) and `data.csv` (version 1) in commit
C1.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/naive_1.dot >}}
```

2. Next we commit the updated `report.Rmd` (version 2) to C2, as well as 
`data.csv`. Note since no changes are made to `data.csv`, it is still at 
version 1.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/naive_2.dot >}}
```

3. Finally, for commit C3, we committed the updated `report.Rmd` (version 3) and
the unchanged `data.csv` (version 1).

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/naive_3.dot >}}
```
:::

(Review the above Git history to see how commits are made step-by-step)

Each commit points to two files in the storage, `report.Rmd` and `data.csv`.
Recall that in this example, all changes are exclusively made in `report.Rmd`, 
while `data.csv` remained unchanged (as raw data should). We are storing
three *identical* `data.csv` that hasn't been changed since commit C1!

To fix this, Git simply keep one copy of `data.csv` in it's storage, and
points all three commits to this `data.csv`:

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/snapshot_0.dot >}}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
# View Full Git History

1. First we commit `report.Rmd` (version 1) and `data.csv` (version 1) in commit
C1.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/snapshot_1.dot >}}
```

2. Next we commit the updated `report.Rmd` (version 2) to C2. Note that since
no changes are made to `data.csv`, instead of creating an identical `data.csv`,
commit C2 simply points to the one that commit C1 created.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/snapshot_2.dot >}}
```

3. Finally, for commit C3, we committed the updated `report.Rmd` (version 3),
and points to the same `data.csv` commit C1 created.


```{dot}
{{< include graphs/snapshot_3.dot >}}
```
:::

Let's hop back to our time machine and see how it behave this time.

If we travel to commit C1, we see version 1 of `Report.Rmd` and `data.csv`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/snapshot_travel_1.dot >}}
```

When we travel to commit C2, we see version 2 of `report.Rmd`, but version 1 of
`data.csv`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/snapshot_travel_2.dot >}}
```
When we travel to commit C3, we see version 3 of `report.Rmd`, and version 1 of
`data.csv`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/snapshot_travel_3.dot >}}
```

This is known as **immutable snapshots**. While users do mutate the files, Git 
never mutate files in its storage. If Git detect changes made to the files, it
add the new file to the storage. If not, it simply points to the old one.

## Diffing

Immutable snapshots makes comparing commits straightforward. We often want to 
track the changes made to a file throughout its development phases, and to do 
so Git can simply compare the files each commit points to and summarize the
changes. This is known as **diffing**.

Consider the `todo.txt` example. Comparing commit C3 to C1 is simply comparing 
`todo.txt` version 3 to version 1.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/diff_todo.dot >}}
```

Git will run a special programme to compare the two files, and calculate the
steps to turn `todo.txt` from version 1 to version 3. Eventually Git would 
produce a diff that looks like:

```diff
 grocery:
-  apple
   banana
+  orange
+clean:
+  dishes
+  laundry
```

Lines that were removed are denoted with minus sign `-` and those that were 
added are prefixed with plus sign `+`. The diff above shows that we remove the
line containing `apple`, and add the line with `orange`, as well as the 3 lines 
involving `clean`.

Note that file diffing is line-based -- a change operating is either removing 
or adding a line. There is no "change line $i$ from $A$ to $B$". 

Say we change `banana` to `banaan`, our diff would look like:

```diff
 grocery:
   apple
-  banana
+  banaan
   orange
 clean:
   dishes
   laundry
```

Git couldn't tell we swapped the last two characters for `banana`. All it can 
say is we deleted the line containing `banana`, and added another line 
containing `banaan`.

Things get more interesting when commits contain more than one files. Let's 
revisit `my-project` example. To compare commit C3 to C1, Git first look at 
`report.Rmd` version 3 and version 1, then calculate the difference as usual. 
Next it move on to `data.csv`, and found both commits points to the same file 
in the storage. No diffing is required for this file!

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/diff_report.dot >}}
```

## Feature branches

Code should be organized based on their functionalities. Instead of writing 
everything in one single file, it is a good practice to split them into smaller
chucks of code across several files. It’s much easier to understand what four 
500-line sections of code are doing than to read through the entire 2,000 lines 
at once.

Consider the following data analysis project.

```
my-project/
├── data/
│   └── survey.csv 
├── results/
│   └── clean_survery.csv
├── clean.R
├── model.R
└── report.Rmd
```

This structure separates codes according to the different phases of data 
pipeline:

1. **Clean data**: `clean.R` reads and cleans raw data `survery.csv`, and 
generate a new dataset `clean_survery.csv`.
2. **Build models**: `model.R` reads `clean_survery.csv` and perform 
statistical analysis.
3. **Present findings**: `report.Rmd` contains the full report where we 
introduce are analysis method and import models from `model.R`.

Assuming our workflow is perfectly linear, that is, for each iteration, we only
add new files and never revise what we have written. Our Git history would look
like:

1. We start with only the raw dataset `survery.csv` in commit C1.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/ideal_1.dot >}}
```

2. We write `clean.R` that takes `survey.csv` as an input, clean it, and
output `clean_survey.R`. Commit C2 points to the newly added `clean.R` and
`clean_survey.R`, as well as `survey.csv` from the previous commit.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/ideal_2.dot >}}
```

3. We build our models in `model.R`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/ideal_3.dot >}}
```



4. Next, we build our models in `models.R` where we take `clean_survey.csv` as
an input. Commit C3 now points to the new file `models.R` and all the files from
previous commits.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/ideal_4.dot >}}
```

5. Finally, we work on our `Report.Rmd` where we explain our methods and import 
models from `models.R` to illustrate our analysis result. Commit C4 points to
the new `Report.Rmd` and all files from previous commit.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/ideal_5.dot >}}
```

But this is rarely the case. We sometimes go back and forth the pipeline, and
make changes to files that were previously committed.

A more realistic workflow may look like this:


```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_0.dot >}}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
# View Full Git History
1. We start with `survey.csv`

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_1.dot >}}
```

2. Next we clean the raw data with `clean.R` and output `clean_survey.csv`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_2.dot >}}
```

3. We build are models in `model.R`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_3.dot >}}
```

4. For `report.Rmd`, we first specify our methods, then import models from 
`model.R`. 

But wait! The model shows the average age for student `mean(age)` to
be `95.3`. Something is not right. Upon inspection we discover some missing 
values in the raw data were coded `999` instead of `NA`, and we failed to 
convert them properly during cleaning. We have to update `clean.R` and 
regenerate `clean_survey.csv`.

First we save what we have for `report.R` -- the models we imported may be 
incorrect, but we don't want to toss away what we have wrote.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_4.dot >}}
```

Then we make the necessary changes to `clean.R` and regenerate 
`clean_survey.csv`. Since both files are modified, commit C5 no longer points 
to version 1 of `clean.R` and `clean_survey.csv`, but the updated version. 

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_5.dot >}}
```

5. Before jumping back to `report.Rmd`, we decide to try a new model. Constant 
correlation doesn't seem to be a realistic assumption, so we test more flexible 
structures, and decide to settle with an autoregressive one. We update
`model.R`, and commit the changes.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_6.dot >}}
```

6. Finally, we complete `report.Rmd`

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_7.dot >}}
```
:::

If we look closely what files are changes in each commit, we notice that only
a few are changed at a time. And thanks to our modularized codebase, these 
changes corresponds to one of three themes: data cleaning, model building and
writing report.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/real_red.dot >}}
```

Can we also modularize our git workflow by categorizing commits based on their
functionalities?

To do so, we need to create **git branches**. When you first create a Git 
project, also known as a **Git repository** (or **repor** for short), all our
commits live in the default branch - the `main` branch. To modularize our 
commits like we do with the code files, we have to create new branches and 
diverge from the `main` branch. All our new changes would be isolated in the
new branches without effecting `main`. We merge the changes from the new 
branches back to `main` once we feel ready. 

[^note-main]: You might see people referring to the first branch as the `master`
    branch in other tutorials. The default name in Git is `master` by the time
    of writing, but in recent years some consider the word offensive and [call 
    for the name to be changed](https://public-inbox.org/git/CAOAHyQwyXC1Z3v7BZAC+Bq6JBaM7FvBenA-1fcqeDV==apdWDg@mail.gmail.com/T/#u).
    In 2020, GitHub [renamed the default name to `main`](https://github.com/github/renaming), 
    and [Git would follow suit starting from version 3.0](https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/xmqqh5usmvsd.fsf@gitster.g/),
    which is expected to be released at the end of 2026.
    While I find the entire argument unnecessary, this is not a hill I want to 
    die on. As someone working on his Main Degree in Statistic, my time is 
    better spent on maining my programming skills. `main` won, so let's use it.

If commits living in the same branch can be seen as snapshots of a timeline, 
then different git branches are like parallel universes reflecting alternative 
states of that timeline. All branches reflect a alternative version of the 
`main` timeline, each containing slightly different changes, usually grouped
by a common theme.

Similar to files, our commits can also be classified into three main themes:
report writing, data cleaning and model building. Therefore we create 3 
branches: `report writing`, `data cleaning` and `model building`, and our 
Git workflow may look something like:
a

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/branch_0.dot >}}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
# View Full Git History

1. Commit `M1`

   we create commit `M1` where we commit raw data `survey.csv` to the default 
   branch `main`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/branch_1_m1.dot >}}
```

2. Commit `R1`

   Next we create a new branch `report-writing`, where we work on our 
   `report.Rmd`. Future commits that contains changes to `report.Rmd` should be
   in this branch.
   
   We create `report.Rmd`, specify our methods in the report, and commit it to 
   `R1`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/branch_2_r1.dot >}}
```

3. Commit `C1`

   To clean our raw data, we create a new branch `data-cleaning`. Note that the 
   new branch is forked from `main` and not `report-writing`, since data 
   cleaning doesn't rely on `report.Rmd`.
   
   We write `clean.R`, generate `clean_survey.csv`, and commit both to `C1`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/branch_3_c1.dot >}}
```

4. Commit `B1`

   We create a new branch `model-buidling` to save model-related commits. Since
   model building depends on `clean_survey.csv`, branch `model-buidling` is 
   branched out from `data-cleaning`.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/branch_4_b1.dot >}}
```

5. Commit `C2`

   We found out the data was not properly cleaned, and has to update `clean.R`
   and regenerate `clean_survey.csv`. 

   To do so, we first go back to branch `data-cleaning` (recall that this 
   branch was created specifically to contain changes regarding data cleaning),
   make changes to `clean.R` and regenerate `clean_survey.csv`, and commit them
   to commit `C2`. 

   Note that since `C2` evolved from `C1`, it doesn't not point to `model.R` --
   the file lives in a parallel universe.

```{dot}
{{< include graphs/branch_5_c2.dot >}}
```

6. Commit `B2`

   Now that we updated `clean.R` and `clean_survey.csv` in branch 
   `data-cleaning`, we need the branch `model-building` to be aware of such
   changes so that we can use the updated data in our models.

   To do so, we merge branch `data-cleaning` to `model-building`, and create
   a new commit `B2`. `B2` not points to version 2 of `clean.R` and 
   `clean_survey.csv` instead of version 1.

